chunks: From him, from al-Sayyari, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), he elevated it, saying:

A man came to Umar and his wife were in a dispute. She called him 'Ya Safilat' (O lowly one). He replied to her, 'If he is lowly, then she is divorced.' Umar said to him, 'If you are among those who follow the storytellers and walk around without need and visit the gates of the Sultan, then she is divorced from you.'
Then Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said to him, 'It is not as you said to me.'
Umar said to him, 'Go to him and hear what he will rule for you.' So he went to him.
Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said to him, 'If you do not care what you said and what was said to you, then you are lowly; otherwise, there is no divorce upon you.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on divorce when a husband calls his wife 'lowly' or uses a casual term of endearment/insult?
ai.summary: This hadith highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of *al-‘Urf* (customary understanding) in interpreting divorce declarations, contrasting Umar’s literalist approach with Imam Ali’s nuanced focus on the husband’s intent and the social weight of the term 'Safilat'. It underscores the importance of contextualizing language within the specific cultural milieu of the time, a key differentiator in Shia legal theory. The narrative serves as a foundational precedent for distinguishing between casual speech and binding legal acts in marital disputes.
